title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: equivocation on 'cause' — true/direct vs abusive/indirect; sun illuminates truly, its setting is only abusively cause of darkness
latin: Aequivocatio in hoc vocabulo causae imposuit adversariis nostris, aut saltem suppeditavit illis occasionem imponendi aliis. Nam dupliciter aliquid dici solet causa talis eventus aut effectus: Vere, directe, et proprie, per modum influentis ad producendum effectum; Abusive, indirecte, improprie, per modum non agentis ad prohibendum effectum: Sicuti sol ortu suo vere et proprie causa dicitur cur aer illuminetur; occasu improprie et abusive causa dicitur cur obtenebretur, hoc sensu solummodo, quia sua praesentia tenebras fugasset.
pass_a: Equivocation in this word cause has imposed upon our adversaries, or at least has supplied them occasion of imposing upon others. For in a twofold way something is wont to be called the cause of such an event or effect: Truly, directly, and properly, after the manner of that which influences unto producing the effect; Abusively, indirectly, improperly, after the manner of that which does not act unto prohibiting the effect: As the sun by its rising is truly and properly said to be the cause why the air is illuminated; by its setting it is improperly and abusively said to be the cause why it is darkened, only in this sense, because by its presence it would have put the darkness to flight.
pass_b: Equivocation on the word cause has trapped our adversaries — or at least given them occasion to trap others. Something is called cause of an event or effect in two ways: truly, directly, and properly, as what flows in to produce the effect; abusively, indirectly, improperly, as what does not act to block the effect. So the sun at rising is truly and properly called cause why the air is lit; at setting it is only improperly and abusively called cause why it darkens — merely because its presence would have put darkness to flight.

lemmas.gloss: sun truly causes light; setting only abusively 'causes' dark

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: special grace's gift is productive cause of salvation — its denial is not truly cause of perdition; Aristotle Metaph. 4.2
latin: Ad hunc fere modum, quia gratiae specialis donatio est causa productiva salutis humanae, quidam inducuntur ut cogitent ejusdem gratiae negationem sive defectum esse causam perditionis humanae, utpote quae sua praesentia perditionem hanc impediret. At ipse Philosophus hac de re accuratius loquitur, Metaph. lib. 4. cap. 2. Quod, cum adsit, alicujus causa est, idem cum absit, aliquando dicimus esse causam contrarii. Observanda sunt illa verba Philosophi, aliquando et dicimus. Non dicit illud per absentiam esse causam contrarii, sed nos illud causari vel tanquam causam obtendere, idque aliquando. Hinc influxus gratiae specialis, Divino decreto quibusdam hominibus negatus, obtendi potest vel cogitari ab imperitis ut causa peccati et perditionis eorundem, quia concessus eosdem servasset; sed falso obtenditur, nisi probari possit, vel Deum obligatum fuisse ad talem gratiam praestandam, vel peccata ac perditionem improborum ex illorum innata corruptione, et voluntaria rebellione, tanquam veris ac positivis causis, non manasse.
pass_a: After nearly this manner, because the gift of special grace is the productive cause of human salvation, certain are led to think that the negation or defect of the same grace is the cause of human perdition, inasmuch as by its presence it would hinder this perdition. But the Philosopher himself speaks more accurately of this matter, Metaph. lib. 4. cap. 2. That which, when it is present, is the cause of something, the same when it is absent we sometimes say to be the cause of the contrary. Those words of the Philosopher are to be observed, sometimes and we say. He does not say that it by absence is the cause of the contrary, but that we allege it or put it forward as a cause, and that sometimes. Hence the influx of special grace, denied by Divine decree unto certain men, can be put forward or thought by the unskilled as the cause of their sin and perdition, because if granted it would have saved them; but it is falsely put forward, unless it can be proved either that God was bound to furnish such grace, or that the sins and perdition of the wicked did not flow from their innate corruption and voluntary rebellion as true and positive causes.
pass_b: Much the same way: because the gift of special grace is the productive cause of human salvation, some are led to think its denial or defect is the cause of human perdition — as if by its presence it would have blocked that perdition. But the Philosopher speaks more carefully (Metaph. 4.2): what, when present, is cause of something, we sometimes say, when absent, is cause of the contrary. Note his words: sometimes and we say. He does not say absence itself is cause of the contrary, but that we allege or put it forward as a cause — and only sometimes. So the influx of special grace, denied by divine decree to some, can be held up by the unskilled as cause of their sin and perdition, because if given it would have saved them. That is false unless it can be proved either that God was bound to give such grace, or that the wicked's sins and perdition did not flow from their innate corruption and voluntary rebellion as true positive causes.

lemmas.gloss: special-grace gift produces salvation; denial not true cause of perdition
Aristotle: we sometimes call absence cause of contrary

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: 'God always ready to add further grace if well used' does not break the defense — election is absolute gift; reprobation denies efficacious grace de facto, not hypothetical gift
latin: Porro, quod dicitur, Deum semper paratum esse cuivis homini adjicere gratiam ulteriorem, si bene utatur accepta, atque idcirco neminem reprobasse nisi ex consideratione antecedanea gratiae contemptae, id est, finalis impoenitentiae ac infidelitatis; nullam vim habet ad defensionem nostram infringendam: Primo, quia uti electio non hypotheticam gratiae donationem ponit, sed absolutam et infallibilem, sic reprobatio haud negat hypotheticam gratiae donationem, sub conditione nimirum, si quis hoc aut illud faceret, sed negat gratiam efficacem de facto donandam. Non ergo sequitur, Si Judas hoc aut illud fecisset, obtinuisset ulteriorem gratiam, Ergo non fuit per decretum reprobationis a gratia speciali absolute rejectus.
pass_a: Further, what is said, that God is always prepared to add unto any man further grace, if he well use what is received, and therefore has reprobated no one except from antecedent consideration of despised grace, that is, of final impenitence and unbelief; has no force unto breaking our defense: First, because as election does not posit a hypothetical gift of grace, but an absolute and infallible one, so reprobation does not deny a hypothetical gift of grace, under the condition namely, if someone should do this or that, but denies efficacious grace to be given in fact. It does not therefore follow, If Judas had done this or that, he would have obtained further grace, Therefore he was not by the decree of reprobation absolutely rejected from special grace.
pass_b: Further: the claim that God is always ready to add further grace to anyone who uses well what he has received — and therefore reprobated no one except from prior regard to despised grace, that is final impenitence and unbelief — has no force to break our defense. First: as election does not posit a hypothetical gift of grace but an absolute infallible one, so reprobation does not deny a hypothetical gift (if someone should do this or that), but denies efficacious grace actually to be given. It does not follow: If Judas had done this or that, he would have obtained further grace; therefore he was not by the reprobation decree absolutely rejected from special grace.

lemmas.gloss: further-grace-if-well-used does not refute absolute reprobation
reprobation denies factual efficacious gift, not hypothetical

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: contempt of given grace may explain withdrawal — not why special mercy that always removes contempt was never prepared; urging the non-reprobate until regeneration
latin: Secundo, contemptus gratiae datae qualiscunque potest recte assignari ut causa cur eadem subducatur, vel cur uberior non administretur; atque hoc ex allatis Scripturae locis evincitur: sed non potest nisi inepte allegari ut causa vel ratio cur specialis illa misericordia, et efficax ac secundum propositum vocatio, quae contemptum gratiae semper tollit, non fuerit huic aut illi praeparata et donata. Hoc ipsum, velle arripere hanc causam ad denegandam gratiam ulteriorem, est non-electionis sive reprobationis antecedaneae manifestum argumentum. Nam quos Deus non reprobavit, eos quamvis multa obstacula ponentes, et sua multiplici negligentia et resistentia gratiae obtationem promerentes, ex indebita tamen et speciali misericordia iterum iterumque urget, nec desistit donec eos regeneraverit et gratiae suae subjugaverit.
pass_a: Secondly, contempt of grace given of whatever sort can rightly be assigned as the cause why the same is withdrawn, or why richer is not administered; and this is proved from the Scripture places alleged: but it cannot except ineptly be alleged as the cause or reason why that special mercy, and efficacious calling according to purpose, which always takes away contempt of grace, was not prepared and given unto this or that one. This very thing, to will to snatch this cause unto denying further grace, is a manifest argument of non-election or antecedent reprobation. For those whom God has not reprobated, them, although putting many obstacles, and by their manifold negligence and resistance deserving the taking-away of grace, yet from undue and special mercy he urges again and again, nor desists until he has regenerated them and subjected them unto his grace.
pass_b: Second: contempt of whatever grace is given can rightly be named as cause why that grace is withdrawn, or why richer grace is not administered — and the cited Scriptures prove that. But it can only be alleged ineptly as cause or reason why that special mercy, and efficacious calling according to purpose which always removes contempt of grace, was never prepared and given to this or that person. To seize on that as the ground for denying further grace is itself a clear mark of non-election or antecedent reprobation. Those God has not reprobated — though they set many obstacles and by manifold negligence and resistance deserve grace to be taken away — he still from undue special mercy urges again and again, and does not stop until he has regenerated them and brought them under his grace.

lemmas.gloss: contempt explains withdrawal, not denial of electing mercy

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: Corvinus's rule 'to him who does all he can by received grace, further grace is always given' does not shake absolute reprobation — no mortal ever does all he can
latin: Tertio, Regula illa, Bene utenti gratia (hoc est, ut exponit Corvinus, pag. 157, facienti quodcunque per gratiam sibi collatam potest facere) dabitur semper gratia ulterior, absolutum decretum reprobationis non labefactat. Quaero enim, Quis mortalium unquam fecit aut facturus est quodcunque per gratiam sibi collatam potest facere? Non fecerunt Angeli; non fecerunt primi parentes; nemo denique electorum post gratiam regenerationis acceptam hoc facit; nedum ut facere id putemus ullum ex non-renatis gratia solummodo excitante instructum, quam a junce naturae vivae distinguit Corvinus.
pass_a: Thirdly, That rule, Unto him that well uses grace (that is, as Corvinus expounds, pag. 157, unto him that does whatsoever by the grace conferred upon him he can do) further grace shall always be given, does not shake the absolute decree of reprobation. For I ask, Who of mortals has ever done or is about to do whatsoever by the grace conferred upon him he can do? The Angels did not; the first parents did not; finally none of the elect after grace of regeneration received does this; much less should we think any of the non-regenerate, furnished only with exciting grace, which Corvinus distinguishes from the living spark of nature, does it.
pass_b: Third: the rule To him who uses grace well (that is, as Corvinus expounds, p. 157, to him who does whatever he can by the grace conferred on him) further grace shall always be given does not shake the absolute decree of reprobation. Who among mortals has ever done, or will ever do, whatever he can by the grace given him? The angels did not; the first parents did not; none of the elect after receiving regenerating grace does it — still less any of the non-regenerate, armed only with exciting grace, which Corvinus distinguishes from the living spark of nature.

lemmas.gloss: no mortal ever does all he can by grace

title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: Thomas — free will disordered toward evil cannot offer no impediment to grace; God sometimes converts even those who impede; the difference hangs on simple will
latin: Multo melius hac de re philosophatur Thomas, qui docet, in libero arbitrio per inordinationem praecedentem ad malum inclinato, non esse situm ut nullum impedimentum gratiae Divinae praestet, Contra Gent. l. 3. c. 160. Deinde adjungit, cap. 161. Deum tamen interdum ex abundantia bonitatis suae eos etiam qui impedimentum gratiae praestant, avertere a malo, et convertere ad bonum. Tandem et illud addit, Hoc fieri in illis solis, in quibus vult suam misericordiam apparere, ita quod in aliis omnibus justitiae ordo manifestetur. Hujus autem discriminis, quare hos ponentes obicem convertat, alios non convertat, rationem inquirendam non esse, quia dependet ex simplici ejus voluntate. Frustra igitur Corvinus ex eo reprobationem impugnat, quod Deus paratus sit uberiorem gratiam dare illis omnibus, qui ita utuntur gratia accepta, ut faciant quodcunque per eam possunt facere, cum nemo hoc praestet, et cum hoc ipsum, non finaliter opponere obicem gratiae Divinae, ex electione dimanet, non autem praecedat electionem.
pass_a: Thomas philosophizes much better of this matter, who teaches that in free will inclined unto evil by a preceding inordination, it is not seated that it should offer no impediment unto Divine grace, Contra Gent. l. 3. c. 160. Then he adds, cap. 161. that God nevertheless sometimes from the abundance of his goodness turns even those who offer an impediment unto grace away from evil, and converts them unto good. At length he also adds that this is done in those alone in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in all others the order of justice may be manifested. But of this discrimination, why he converts these putting an obstacle, others he does not convert, the reason is not to be sought, because it depends upon his simple will. In vain therefore does Corvinus impugn reprobation from this, that God is prepared to give richer grace unto all those who so use received grace that they do whatsoever by it they can do, since no one performs this, and since this very thing, not finally to oppose an obstacle unto Divine grace, flows from election, and does not precede election.
pass_b: Thomas reasons far better here. He teaches that free will, already disordered toward evil, is not so set that it offers no impediment to divine grace (Contra Gent. 3.160). Then (cap. 161) he adds that God nonetheless sometimes, from abundance of his goodness, turns even those who impede grace away from evil and converts them to good — and that this happens only in those in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in all others the order of justice is shown. Why he converts these who put an obstacle and not others is not to be sought; it hangs on his simple will. So Corvinus vainly attacks reprobation from God's readiness to give richer grace to all who use received grace so as to do whatever they can by it — since no one does that, and since not finally opposing an obstacle to divine grace itself flows from election and does not precede election.

lemmas.gloss: disordered will impedes; God sometimes converts anyway
not finally opposing grace flows from election
